```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 144, out.width = "100%", dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg",
  dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
PAL <- c(blue = "#2E6F9E", red = "#B5342B", green = "#3F7A3D",
         orange = "#9E5E0F", purple = "#7A4F9E", teal = "#2A7A7A",
         grey = "#5C6166")
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 17) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.key = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.position = "none"))
```

A three-dimensional panel often needs two-dimensional companions: ordinary ggplot2 layers drawn inside it, flat projections of the data on the floor and walls of the box, or a contour map and a profile next to it. This article shows each of these, then arranges 3D panels with 2D panels using a second package. Installation is covered in [Get started](ggplot3d.html). The composition sections also use [patchwork](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com), the package that arranges several ggplot2 plots on one page.

```{r packages, message=FALSE}
library(patchwork)
```

## Plain ggplot2 layers in a 3D panel

The data below trace a helix. `track` contains an angle `t`, the positions `x` and `y` on a unit circle, and a height `z` that rises from 1 to 3 over two turns. The ends are labelled in a second table.

```{r helix-data}
track <- data.frame(t = seq(0, 4 * pi, length.out = 80))
track$x <- cos(track$t)
track$y <- sin(track$t)
track$z <- 1 + track$t / (2 * pi)
ends <- track[c(1, nrow(track)), ]
ends$label <- c("start", "end")
```

`geom_path()`, `geom_point()` and `geom_text()` are the ggplot2 layers, used unchanged. Inside `coord_3d()` they read the z mapping and are placed and depth sorted like `geom_path_3d()`, `geom_point_3d()` and `geom_text_3d()`.

```{r plain-layers, fig.alt="A blue helix rising through two turns, with red points and the labels start and end at its two ends."}
h <- ggplot(track, aes(x, y, z = z))
h + geom_path(colour = PAL["blue"], linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = ends, colour = PAL["red"], size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), data = ends, nudge_x = 0.35, size = 5) +
  coord_3d()
```

The accepted ggplot2 geoms are points, paths, lines, segments, text, labels, polygons, rectangles, tiles, `geom_hline()`, `geom_vline()`, `annotation_custom()`, `annotation_raster()` and `geom_blank()`; `geom_contour()` and `geom_density_2d()` draw each line at the height of its level. A layer without a z mapping is drawn at z = 0, and the z scale extends to include 0. Here the path is drawn a second time with `inherit.aes = FALSE`, so it lies flat at height 0 below the helix.

```{r z-zero, fig.alt="The blue helix above a grey circle drawn at height zero; the z axis now starts at zero."}
h + geom_path(colour = PAL["blue"], linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_path(aes(x, y), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = PAL["grey"],
            linewidth = 0.8) +
  coord_3d()
```

## Projecting points onto the floor and walls

A position of `-Inf` or `Inf` places a mark on the matching face of the box, as `Inf` places a mark on the panel edge in ggplot2. The cloud below has 40 points whose height follows `x + y` with noise.

```{r cloud-data}
set.seed(1)
cloud <- data.frame(x = rnorm(40), y = rnorm(40))
cloud$z <- cloud$x + cloud$y + rnorm(40, sd = 0.5)
```

Mapping `z = -Inf` draws each point's shadow on the floor, and a dropline joins each point to it. Mapping `y = Inf` draws the projection onto the back wall at the largest y, where the points show z against x.

```{r projections, fig.alt="Forty dark points in a box, grey shadows on the floor joined to them by vertical lines, and orange projections on the back wall."}
k <- ggplot(cloud, aes(x, y, z = z))
k + geom_point_3d(aes(z = -Inf), colour = PAL["grey"], size = 1.5) +
  geom_point_3d(aes(y = Inf), colour = PAL["orange"], size = 1.5) +
  geom_dropline_3d(face = "zmin", colour = PAL["grey"]) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 2.5) +
  coord_3d()
```

Shadows and wall projections use the same x, y and z scales as the points, so each projection lies on the box grid at the coordinates it shares with its point. The scales are trained on the finite positions only, so the box keeps the range of the data.

## Reference lines and annotations

`geom_hline()` and `geom_vline()` draw a line across the box at height 0, here the two zero lines of x and y. `annotate()` has no z position; `annotate_3d()` takes the same arguments as `annotate()` together with `z`, `zmin`, `zmax` and `zend`. Here it labels the highest point of the cloud.

```{r annotations, fig.alt="Forty dark points in a box, two grey lines crossing at x = 0 and y = 0 at height zero, and a white label reading highest next to the top point."}
top <- cloud[which.max(cloud$z), ]
k + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL["grey"]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = PAL["grey"]) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 2.5) +
  annotate_3d("label", x = top$x, y = top$y, z = top$z, label = "highest",
              hjust = -0.15) +
  coord_3d()
```

The label is a box drawn at the projected position of its point; points and faces in front of that position cover it.

## Contours and densities on the floor

The surface below has a peak and a hollow. `surface` contains one row for each of 25 by 25 grid positions with the height `z`.

```{r surface-data}
surface <- expand.grid(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 25),
                       y = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 25))
surface$z <- with(surface, exp(-((x - 0.5)^2 + y^2)) -
  0.6 * exp(-((x + 0.8)^2 + (y + 0.6)^2) / 0.5))
```

`geom_contour_filled_3d()` with `plane = "floor"` computes height bands from the same grid and draws them flat on the floor, giving a contour map under the surface. A higher camera elevation shows more of the floor.

```{r floor-contours, fig.alt="A grey surface with a peak and a hollow above a floor coloured in six height bands, light for low and dark blue for high."}
ramp <- c("#DCEAF3", PAL[["blue"]])
s <- ggplot(surface, aes(x, y, z = z))
s + geom_contour_filled_3d(plane = "floor", bins = 6) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey85") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = ramp[1], high = ramp[2]) +
  coord_3d(elevation = 40)
```

The bands are computed in the same z units as the surface, so the darkest band on the floor sits under the peak and the lightest under the hollow.

A density surface can stand over the observations it was estimated from. `faithful` records the duration and the waiting time of 272 eruptions of the Old Faithful geyser. `stat_density_2d_3d()` draws the estimated density, and the eruptions are drawn on the floor with `z = -Inf`. The surface is half transparent and the camera is raised, so the points under the two peaks show through. The z title is set with `labs()` because the density layer computes z and has no z mapping to name it.

```{r density-floor, fig.alt="A half-transparent grey density surface with two peaks over the faithful data, with the 272 eruptions drawn as black points on the floor below the peaks."}
ggplot(faithful, aes(eruptions, waiting)) +
  stat_density_2d_3d(n = 24, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point_3d(aes(z = -Inf), size = 1) +
  labs(z = "density") +
  coord_3d(elevation = 50)
```

With `plane = "floor"`, `stat_density_2d_3d()` lays the same density grid flat on the floor and fills it by density, a heat map under the surface.

```{r density-heat, fig.alt="The half-transparent grey density surface over a floor coloured from dark blue where the density is low to light blue under the two peaks."}
ggplot(faithful, aes(eruptions, waiting)) +
  stat_density_2d_3d(n = 24, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_density_2d_3d(n = 48, plane = "floor") +
  labs(z = "density") +
  coord_3d(elevation = 50)
```

## A 3D panel beside 2D panels

A ggplot3d plot is a ggplot object, so patchwork arranges it with 2D plots. The surface is coloured by height and stacked above a 2D raster of the same grid. Both plots use the same fill scale, so `guides = "collect"` draws one legend for both.

```{r shared-scale, fig.height=8, fig.alt="Top, the surface coloured from red in the hollow to blue at the peak; bottom, the same grid as a flat raster map in the same colours; one shared colour bar for height."}
heights <- scale_fill_gradient2(low = PAL["red"], mid = "#F2F2F2",
  high = PAL["blue"], limits = c(-0.6, 1), name = "z")
top <- s + stat_surface_3d(aes(fill = after_stat(z_mean))) +
  heights + coord_3d()
map <- ggplot(surface, aes(x, y, fill = z)) + geom_raster() +
  heights + coord_equal()
top / map + plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

The 3D panel colours each triangle by its mean height, and the raster colours each grid cell by its height. The colours agree because the two plots share the limits of `heights`.

A profile shows one line of the surface at full resolution. `profile` contains the grid rows with y = 0. The same rows are drawn as a red path on the 3D surface and as a 2D line against x.

```{r profile, fig.height=8, fig.alt="Top, the grey surface with a red line running across it at y equal to zero; bottom, the same red line as a 2D profile of z against x."}
profile <- surface[abs(surface$y) < 1e-9, ]
across <- s + geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey85") +
  geom_path_3d(data = profile, colour = PAL["red"], linewidth = 1) +
  coord_3d()
side <- ggplot(profile, aes(x, z)) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL["red"], linewidth = 1)
across / side
```

The x axis has the same range in both panels, so the hollow near x = -1 and the peak near x = 0.5 appear at the same x in the path and in the profile.

## Two camera views of one plot

The camera arguments of `coord_3d()` take one value per panel. To show the same data from two directions, repeat the data once per view, facet by the view, and give each panel its own angles.

```{r two-views, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.5, fig.alt="Two panels: the grey surface from the default view, and the same surface seen from a higher camera on the opposite side."}
views <- rbind(transform(surface, view = "default view"),
               transform(surface, view = "from the opposite side"))
ggplot(views, aes(x, y, z = z)) + geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey85") +
  facet_wrap(~view) +
  coord_3d(azimuth = c(-60, 120), elevation = c(30, 55))
```

Both panels keep one magnification, so the surface has the same size in each. Separate plots with their own `coord_3d()`, arranged with patchwork, do the same for plots with different data.

```{r two-plots, fig.height=8, fig.alt="The grey surface from the default view above the same surface seen from a higher camera on the opposite side."}
base <- s + geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey85")
(base + coord_3d()) /
  (base + coord_3d(azimuth = 120, elevation = 55))
```

[Camera and framing](camera.html) describes the angles. [The z scale](z-scale.html) shows facets with fixed and free z ranges.

## Titles and captions

Titles, subtitles and captions are drawn outside the panel in page coordinates, as in any ggplot2 plot.

```{r titles, fig.alt="The grey surface with the title Two Gaussian features, a subtitle giving the positions of the peak and the hollow, and a caption below the panel."}
base + coord_3d() +
  labs(title = "Two Gaussian features",
       subtitle = "Peak near (0.5, 0), hollow near (-0.8, -0.6)",
       caption = "Heights on a 25 by 25 grid")
```

In a patchwork layout the same `labs()` call names one panel, and `plot_annotation()` adds a title over the whole arrangement.

```{r layout-title, fig.height=8, fig.alt="The surface with its red profile line above the 2D profile, under the overall title Profile at y = 0."}
across / side + plot_annotation(title = "Profile at y = 0")
```
